title: How we used AI to make repeat runs less repetitive in a mobile life sim
author: GoldtusksStudio
selftext:
I’m the developer behind Nirvana: Game of Life. The original game is a hand-designed swipe-based life simulator; the new mobile feature adds AI-generated life events based on real-world content rather than generating the entire game.



The design problem we were solving was repetition: after several runs, players could start seeing the same patterns. The AI layer is meant to expand event variety while the core choices and consequences stay authored and playable.

If you’ve shipped AI content in an existing game, how do you balance novelty with consistency?

comments.author: RoyalSpecialist1777
comments.body:
First thought would be to keep the authored storyline and endings, but represent the game underneath as a directed, mostly non-cyclic graph of abstract story beats.

Each node would represent something like "career opportunity," "relationship crisis," "financial setback," etc., rather than a specific card. You could then have a dozen or more different card pairs that instantiate the same underlying node and move the player roughly the same direction.

The individual cards could still set flags that open or close later paths and card options, so two players might pass through the same broad story beat but have different downstream options. Paths can branch and reconverge at important points, with the existing endings remaining the terminal nodes.

That seems like it would give you a lot more variety without letting the AI take over the actual game design. The AI could generate new realizations of an existing abstract event, possibly using the player's current state and real-world material, while the allowed choices, consequences, path changes, and endings remain authored.

Basically use AI to expand the number of ways the existing game can be expressed, rather than having it invent the structure of the game itself.
